title: I built an AI RPG where the LLM isn't allowed to control the game state. Has anyone else tried this?
author: -TheFlea-
selftext:
I built an AI RPG where the LLM is not allowed to control the game state. Has anyone else tried this architecture?

Most AI RPG implementations I've seen seem to give the language model enormous authority: it receives the current situation, generates what happens next, and the generated narrative effectively becomes reality.

I went in the opposite direction.

I built a playable RPG where the LLM is primarily an interpreter and narrator operating around a separate canonical game state.

The basic rule is:

The model can describe reality. It cannot simply make reality true by saying it.

Player input arrives as unrestricted natural language. The system has to distinguish between what the player actually authorized and things the model might merely infer.

For example:

“I look around for somebody who might be hiring.”

does not authorize:

\- approaching somebody

\- starting a conversation

\- accepting work

\- traveling somewhere

\- deciding how the player character feels

The world state, NPC knowledge, relationships, time, money, resources and consequences persist separately from the prose.

NPCs also have bounded knowledge and their own state rather than automatically knowing whatever the narrator knows.

Uncertainty is resolved separately as well, so the narrator can't simply choose the outcome that produces the nicest story.

The difficult part has been making all of that work while still allowing the player to type essentially arbitrary actions rather than selecting from a predetermined menu.

I am not a programmer by training. I designed the system and used AI coding tools heavily to implement it. The first playable version is now running.

What I'm trying to understand is whether other people working with LLMs in games have converged on a similar separation between:

semantic interpretation → canonical state → resolution → narration

rather than letting the LLM itself function as the source of truth.

Has anyone here built or experimented with something similar?

comments.author: JedahVoulThur
comments.body:
I have also noticed that a lot of aidevs use LLMs the same unimaginative ways.
I just launched a game in which the LLM is only used to respond to the player inputs, it has no more responsibility than that and still it is very controlled through a Behavior Tree and Regex.

In a different project I'm working on, I will use the LLM to analyze its environment and take decisions other systems interpret and execute.
